newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal vote held up by absent deputies controversy.
newsitem.headline: Nepal vote held up by absent deputies controversy.

text.p: Nepal's communist led opposition remained adamant on Tuesday that a no-confidence motion would not proceed until the government explains the absence of some deputies expected to vote against it.

The opposition alleged that the government had forcibly kept away deputies, including some of its own ministers, who were likely to vote against Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba's 15-month-old, centre-right coalition.

"They should come up with their explanations. Without that we will not allow the proceedings to go on," Devi Prasad Ojha, chief whip of the main opposition Unified Marxist Leninist party, told Reuters.
Deuba was due to reply to the no-confidence motion before the vote can be carried out.
Parliament was expected to reconvene earlier on Tuesday after speaker Ram Chandra Poudel adjourned an unruly late night session in the Himalayan kingdom.
But before resuming, Poudel met representatives of the main parties to discuss the whereabouts of the missing deputies and the reason for their absence, parliament officials said.

Almost the entire opposition staged a four hour sit-in in the central aisle of the lower house and snatched away the speaker's microphone to stop efforts to push through the vote during a session that ended in the early hours of Tuesday.

The opposition said five government ministers and one deputy each from two minor parties, the Nepal Workers and Peasants Party (NWPP) and the Nepal Sadbhavana Party (NSP), were kept away by the government for fear that they would vote against it.

The NWPP announced earlier in the day that its three deputies would vote against the government. The chief of the NSP is a member of the government, but two remaining deputies of his party had said they would vote against the coalition.
"One of my three deputies is missing since the morning from his residence," NWPP president Narayan Man Bijukuchhe said on Monday.

"Five ministers were sent to Bangkok for fear that they will vote against the government," said former minister Kamal Thapa of the Rashtriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), who resigned from the coalition last week to campaign against the government.
Deuba denied any wrongdoing and said the ministers had gone to Bangkok for medical treatment.
Constituents of the coalition are divided over support for the government.
NWPP's support for the no-confidence motion, moved on Saturday by the UML, had increased the chances that the government would lose a close-run vote, politicians said.
Deuba's three-party coalition commands 108 of the 205 house seats. Of this, Deuba's Nepali Congress has 86 members and the RPP 19. But the RPP is sharply divided.

The split in the RPP prompted the communist UML to move the no-confidence vote against Deuba's coalition. The UML, which failed to remove Deuba in a no-confidence vote last March, are hoping the RPP will break away from the Nepali Congress.
Politicians estimated that the decision by NWPP would raise the number of votes in support of the motion to 104, just above the 103 required to pass it.

Deuba's Nepali Congress was demanding disqualification of the two defecting NSP members, which would cost the opposition two crucial votes. But one of the two NSP members was not in the house and this sparked protests.
